title: Montana BOPA — 20200229 Recommendation IAFF HAVRE FF
text:
IN THE MATTER OF FACTFINDING
BEFORE FACTFINDER JEFF J. MINCKLER
BOPA No. 20200229:
INTERNATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF
FIRE FIGHTERS,
FINDINGS
Union,
AND
and
RECOMMENDATIONS
CITY OF HAVRE, MONTANA,
Employer.
ISSUED DECEMBER 22, 2020
é é é é é é é é é é é é é é é é é
ISSUES IN DISPUTE
Union:
Base wage rate for fiscal years 2017-2018 and 2018-2019.
Health insurance tier structure and contributions.
Callback time on all emergent ambulance transfers.
Employer:
Base wage rate for fiscal years 2018-2019 and 2019-2020.
Health insurance program and contributions.
HEARING
November 13, 2020, 10:00 AM MST, via Zoom videoconference
APPEARANCES
Union: Tim Hoover, IAFF District 5 Representative, Seattle, Washington
Employer: Jean E. Faure, Faure Holden, Great Falls, Montana
RECOMMENDATIONS
Base wage: Union's proposed 4.0% retroactive increase through June 30, 2019.
Health insurance tier structure and contributions: Union's proposed status quo.
Nonemergent callback: Union's proposal.

1 A. OPINION
2 1. INTRODUCTION
3 On March 5, 2020, I received an appointment by the parties above to serve as
4 the sole factfinder to conduct a hearing and issue recommendations on the matters
5 before me. I promptly contacted each party and each subsequently authorized me
6 to determine all procedural matters, to arrange and conduct a hearing, and to
7 issue recommendations. Because for many years I represented the City of Havre
8 in labor relations matters involving the Firefighters' bargaining unit, both parties
9 waived conflict of interest and all other possible objections relative to that past
10 involvement.
11 The hearing was originally scheduled for June 5, 2020 in Havre, Montana, but
12 was postponed twice due to concerns over the COVID-19 virus. It was eventually
13 conducted via videoconference on November 13, 2020 beginning at 10:00 AM MST.
14 Both parties were present and participated and argument, evidence and testimony
15 were received after witnesses were sworn. Evidence was in the form of documents
16 which were assessed on their relevance and reliability; and testimony which was
17 assessed on each witness's capacity to observe, character and demeanor, bias,
18 inconsistent statements, credible contradiction, and the reasonableness of his or
19 her testimony.
20 At the conclusion of the hearing each party stipulated it had been given a full
21 opportunity to present all the evidence it considered pertinent.
22 39-31-309(6), MCA allows a factfinder to attempt to mediate the dispute. After
23 reviewing the history of negotiations and becoming convinced the parties had thor-
24 oughly explored options, I did not.
25 39-31-309(4), MCA requires a factfinder issue written findings of facts and rec-
26 ommendations for resolution of the disputes no later than 20 days from the end of
27 the hearing. The parties requested the opportunity to file briefs by November 30,
28 2020, so in this case the required date for issuing my recommendations was De-
29 cember 29, 2020. However, due to a staff illness and a computer problem, the
BOPA No. 20200229 1. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 parties agreed to extend the briefing deadline to December 2, 2020, making De-
2 cember 31, 2020 the date by which my recommendations are to be issued.
3 After conducting a hearing and reviewing all testimony, evidence and the briefs,
4 the following is issued.
5 2. ISSUES
6 The parties declared the following to be all of their unresolved final proposals:
7 From the Employer:
8
9 1. FY 2018-2019: 2.0% wage increase, not retroactive.
10
11 2. FY 2019-2020: 2.0% wage increase, retroactive.
12
13 3. Health insurance: Full payment of health and dental premiums for the
14 employee, with spouse and family plans available to those hired before
15 ratification.
16
17 From the Union:
18
19 1. Article 11 - Wages and other compensation: (i) (A) Wages: 4.0% increase
20 on base wage applied throughout the matrix in Addendum A, with all
21 applicable pay and benefits adjusted, retroactive to July 1, 2017.
22
23 2. Article 11 - Wages and other compensation: (ii) (New section after E) Non-
24 emergent Callback: Three hours of minimum callback time on all non-
25 emergent ambulance transfers, paid at time and one-half the employee's
26 regular rate of pay regardless if such constitutes overtime.
27
28 3. Article 31 - Duration of agreement: Expiration date of June 30, 2019.
29
30 3. POSITIONS
31 Employer:
32 Negotiations for a contract with a term beginning July 1, 2018 have been ongo-
33 ing since early 2018. In November 2019 the parties participated in mediation which
34 was unsuccessful. Negotiations continued until the Union petitioned for factfind-
35 ing.
36 For many years the Employer provided a contribution toward each participating
37 employee's health and dental insurance premium as well as for each covered family
38 member. In 2017 the Employer and its three bargaining units conducted a review
BOPA No. 20200229 2. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 of the City's insurance program. Based on the desire of many employees to convert
2 some of the City's insurance contributions to wages, the City decided to fix its
3 contribution toward insurance premiums for existing employees and covered fam-
4 ily members. For employees hired after 2017, the City pays the full premium cost
5 for participating employees, but it pays nothing toward premium costs for family
6 members.
7 Two of the three bargaining units accepted these changes, but not the Firefight-
8 ers' unit which challenged the City's action in arbitration. The Union won, so the
9 City has continued to contribute all but $52.95 for each participating firefighter,
10 all but $246.50 for each firefighter selecting the two-party plan, and all but
11 $328.75 for each firefighter selecting the family plan. The sum of these contribu-
12 tions equates to 4% of the Firefighters' unit's base wage. For 2018, the Employer
13 offered the Firefighters the 4% raise it gave all other employees plus an additional
14 settlement incentive. The total of the Employer's offer to the Firefighters' unit con-
15 stitutes a 6% package increase. The Union's proposal to continue the Employer's
16 insurance premium contributions at 2017 levels, plus the 4% wage increase of-
17 fered by the Employer, would equate to an 8% increase - about double what other
18 City employees received.
19 Montana statutes require an arbitrator to compare compensation provided by
20 the Employer with that of employees performing the same services for other em-
21 ployers, and the parties hereto have directed me to abide by that same require-
22 ment. Montana statutes classify its cities into Class 1 and Class 2, based on pop-
23 ulation, and the City of Havre's population of 9,500 makes it a Class 2 city. How-
24 ever, the city council of a Class 2 city with a population of between 9,000 and
25 10,000 has the option under statute to vote to be deemed a Class 1 city. The City
26 of Havre qualifies to exercise that option, which the Havre City Council has done.
27 This results in Havre being the only Class 1 city with a population under 20,000,
28 making it inappropriate to compare Havre with other Montana Class 1 cities.
29 The Union wishes to compare Havre firefighters with those of Kalispell, Mon-
30 tana, another Class 1 city. However, Kalispell has a population of about 25,000,
BOPA No. 20200229 3. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 compared with Havre's 9,500. The Union is comparing Havre firefighters with a
2 city with a tax base of about double Havre's, with a city that is experiencing high
3 growth, and with a city that has a much higher cost of living. It would be more
4 appropriate to compare Havre with Montana's Class 2 cities. Additionally, Havre
5 differs from Kalispell in that Havre has combined its fire department with its am-
6 bulance service which makes about 1,400 service calls each year.
7 Analyzing the ability of the Employer to afford the Union's proposal must take
8 into account the method for funding the Fire Department. The Havre Fire Depart-
9 ment is funded 70% by the Enterprise fund which gets its revenue partly from
10 proceeds from its ambulance service and partly from tax revenues, and the re-
11 maining 30% by the general fund. For the period 2018-2019, the Fire Department
12 budget was $1,067,000, of which $348,000 or 33% was funded by ambulance ser-
13 vice proceeds, and $719,000 or 67% was funded by tax revenues. Montana stat-
14 utes limit the City's ability to increase city taxes to whatever rate is supportive of
15 the City's conservative budgeting tradition, leaving requesting revenue to cover Fire
16 Department budget shortfalls from only Hill County taxpayers.
17 The Employer has explained to the Union that it cannot address wages without
18 also addressing insurance premium contributions as a package because paying
19 for each of the Union's proposals is not sustainable. For example, health insurance
20 premium costs increased by 4.2% in 2018, and will increase by 8% in 2021.
21 The Factfinder must consider only the City's existing funding ability and he
22 cannot substitute his judgment for the City's budgetary analysis and philosophy.
23 Union:
24 Havre is the 8th largest city in Montana in the terms of population. The Fire
25 Department serves not only the 38 square miles that constitute the City of Havre,
26 but 1,347 square miles of Hill County in addition. The City also provides medical
27 transport to Great Falls, Montana, which is 115 miles south of Havre.
28 Contract negotiations with the Employer have been ongoing since early 2018,
29 and included a hold while an arbitrator decided a unilateral change in insurance
30 contribution issue, and an unsuccessful mediation. Havre firefighters are the
BOPA No. 20200229 4. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 lowest paid of any of Montana's 7 other Class 1 fire departments, and the Union's
2 proposal for a 4% wage increase would still compensate Havre firefighters 15%
3 below the next highest Montana Class 1 fire department. Negotiations for a 2015
4 CBA ended in interest arbitration with Arbitrator Larney agreeing with the Union
5 that comparing Havre firefighters to other Montana Class 1 firefighters is appro-
6 priate given that the Havre City Council takes the voluntary initiative necessary to
7 be deemed a Class 1 city, and that under statute Havre is very close anyway to
8 being a Class 1 city anyway.
9 The Union also proposes a one hour increase in the call-out time provision in
10 Article 11, Section E, to properly compensate firefighters for the time required be-
11 fore and after making a transfer.
12 The Union's other proposal is for a contract term that expires on June 30, 2019,
13 because although the Union originally proposed a multiyear contract, the Em-
14 ployer has expressed a strong preference for a one-year contract.
15 4. ANALYSIS
16 The parties instructed me to use criteria provided by Montana statute for arbi-
17 trators when assessing each party's final position, and for each unresolved issue
18 to select as my recommendation the unmodified previously established final posi-
19 tion of one of the parties. The statutory criteria is contained in 39-34-103(5), MCA:
20 In arriving at a determination, the arbitrator shall consider any relevant
21 circumstances, including:
22 a. comparison of hours, wages and conditions of employment of the em-
23 ployees involved with employees performing similar services and with
24 other services generally;
25 b. the interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the
26 public employer to pay;
27 c. appropriate cost-of-living indices;
28 d. any other factors considered in the determination of hours, wages, and
29 conditions of employment.
30
31 This statute is unartfully drafted in that it begins formulating criteria with: "...
32 the arbitrator shall consider any relevant circumstances, including ..." [italics
33 added], which appears to make the itemization of criteria which follow as only
34 some of what may be considered. The statute ends: "any other factors considered
BOPA No. 20200229 5. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 in the determination of hours, wages, and conditions of employment." Instead of
2 creating two separate "any other factors" categories, I believe these provisions are
3 operationally redundant and the intent is to provide an arbitrator, or the Fact-
4 finder in this case, the opportunity to consider "relevant factors" other than what
5 the statute itemizes. It is important to have a clear understanding of statutory
6 requirements, but in this case the "any other factors" provisions are moot because
7 I find the factors itemized in Sections a and b sufficient to allow appropriate con-
8 sideration of the proposals and arguments advanced by each party because there
9 was no proposal regarding "cost-of-living indices" or any other factor not embraced
10 by Sections a and b. Taking these two "relevant factors" in order:
11 a. Comparison of hours, wages and conditions of employment of the employees
12 involved with employees performing similar services and with other services gen-
13 erally:
14 Because of significant differences in how countries and U.S. state legislatures
15 structure their municipal governments for several purposes including taxation
16 and compensation, it is common and appropriate to confine wage and benefit
17 comparisons to municipalities in the same country and state in which the local
18 government exists. Montana has 363 separate municipalities with populations
19 between 109,577 in Billings and 10 in Silesia.1 The vast differences between these
20 municipalities makes it is impossible to draft a variety of overarching regulations.
21 Because of this, based on population the State of Montana divides its cities and
22 towns into four classifications under 7-1-4111, MCA, and imposes differing regu-
23 lations based on these classifications:
24 (1) Every city having a population of 10,000 or more is a city of the first
25 class.
26 (2) Every city having a population of less than 10,000 and more than 5,000
27 is a city of the second class.
28 (3) Every city having a population of less than 5,000 and more than 1,000
29 is a city of the third class.
30 (4) Every municipal corporation having a population of less than 1,000 and
31 more than 300 is a town.
1 U.S Census Bureau.
BOPA No. 20200229 6. Factfinding: 2017-2020

1 The obvious question is if Havre firefighters are to be compared with what other
2 Montana municipalities compensate their firefighters, is it more appropriate to
3 compare Havre with all 363 Montana cities and towns, or just those employed by
4 cities of the same classification.
5 When negotiating for a contract in 2014, the parties opted for factfinding and
6 in February 2015 Factfinder Schramm found it appropriate to compare Havre
7 firefighters with other Montana Class 1 and Class 2 governments.2 The parties
8 rejected Schramm's recommendations and invoked interest arbitration. In his de-
9 cision of December 2015, Arbitrator Larney concurred in part with Schramm's
10 analysis but compared Havre firefighters with just those employed by other Mon-
11 tana Class 1 cities,3 partly because Havre, with a current population of 9,791,4
12 would be a Class 2 Montana city under statute except the Havre City Council
13 continuously opts to use the exception provided by 7-1-4112, MCA in order to be
14 deemed a Class 1 Montana city:
15 (1) [E]very municipal corporation having a population of more than 9,000
16 and less than 10,000 may, by resolution adopted by the city council ... be
17 either a first-class city or a second-class city ...".
18
19 The City of Havre realizes benefits from being Class 1 such as the establish-
20 ment and operation of courts (Title 3), the operation of local government (Title 7),
21 taxation powers (Title 15), retirement systems (Title 19), health boards and other
22 health related issues (Title 50), and land use (Title 76). Havre firefighters also
23 benefit from the Council's decision in that Title 7, chapter 33, part 41 requires a
24 Class 1 city to have a fire department consisting of only paid employees while a
25 Class 2 city may augment a paid department with volunteers. Consistent with
26 that requirement, the Havre fire department is wholly comprised of paid employ-
27 ees.
28 I am persuaded by Arbitrator Larney's rationale when he determined that be-
29 cause the Havre City Council opted to be deemed a Montana Class 1 city, and
2 Schramm factfindng recommendations of February 23, 2015.
3 Larney interest arbitration award of December 14, 2015, pp. 9-10.

2 Class 1 city, it be deemed a Class 1 city for the purposes of comparing firefighters'
3 wages and benefits. Therefore, for the purpose of this recommendation I find it
4 appropriate and sufficient to compare the City of Havre with the other Montana
5 Class 1 cities.

8 Havre has a population of 20% of the average of all Montana Class 1 cities, and
9 its population grew from 2018 to 2019 by 20% of the average population change
10 for that period. Dealing for the moment with just wages, fixing Havre's firefighter
11 compensation at 20% of the Class 1 average would be as silly as suggesting Bo-
12 zeman's compensation should be 45% of what Billings pays its firefighters. Fur-
13 ther, a quick look at compensation for firefighters in Montana Class 1 cities indi-
14 cates an absence of any consistent correlation between a city's population and
15 rates of pay. The only logical and appropriate comparison is between the City of
16 Havre and the average of the entire group of Montana Class 1 cities, into which
17 the Havre City Council has opted to place itself.
18 (1) Wages: Part of the Employer's stated objection to the Union's wage proposals
19 center on the increase it provided to its other employees. However, the Employer
20 otherwise argues it is inappropriate for the Factfinder to compare one Havre

4 comparison is between Havre firefighters and those employed by other Montana

16 (3) Nonemergent callback: The Union proposes a new section for the CBA which

29 ning or end of his or her regularly scheduled shift.

17 with an ending date of June 30, 2019, and negotiations for a successive contract.
18 When one party to contract negotiations refuses to extend a potential agree-

1 b. The interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the public
2 employer to pay:
3 This factor is comprised of two separate but related elements: The potential
4 impact of the proposals on the public, and the ability of the employer to fund the
